mission_3.prediction: Increasing repulsion strength made the robot avoid the obstacle more exaggerated. lowering the Influence distance decreased the size of the circle around the obstacle. This made it so that the robot does not begin to avoid the obstacle until it gets closer. Increasing the refinement step increased the strength that our repulsion has on our robot thus listening less to the attraction line. Changing these values did not get my robot stuck. Even with the influence at .6 on sol_1, it does not have to move out of the way and turn. For sol_2, it does turn once it gets within the 1.1 m radius of the person and does quite exaggeratedly.
mission_3.comparison: For A*, soc_2 had the largest minimum_person_cleraance_m at .794m compared to .738 m for baseline, and its personal_space_s dropped from 1.3s to 0. The wider spacing did not cost much more as soc_2 took 46.6s and 13.18m compar3ed to 46.29 s of the baseline. For RRT, the baseline ended with controller_failed (Nav2 error 105, failed to make progress). The completed condition with the largest clearance was social_1 at 1.76 m with 0 s of personal_space_s, while the failed baseline had 1.719 m and also 0 s. social_1 did not cost more as it took 43.5 s and 11.48 m, while the baseline had already used 53.6 s and 11.71 m before it failed.
mission_3.recommendation: I would keep A* with social_2 for this scenario because it  succeeded with a minimum clearance of 0.794 m and took 46.6 s over 13.18 m. Compared to RRT with social_1, which succeeded with a larger clearance of 1.76 m in 43.5 s, I still prefer A* social_2 since A* gives the same route every run while RRT does not. One thing these static-person trials cannot tell us is how the robot would handle a person who walks into its path.
